content.title: Luke Kennard traded from Atlanta to Lakers in latest Duke Trade Deadline move
content.text: (1)Duke vs. (5)St.John's 2026 NCAA East Region SemifinalCapital One Arena, Washington, DCTip Off: 7:10 PM EST on CBSDuke's Sweet 16 game against St. John's looks less like a skills contest and more like a test of control.The Red Storm arrive with a statistical profile and style of play that can make even efficient teams look uncomfortable. The Johnnies press, they force turnovers, they rebound their misses and they get to the foul line. They are older than Duke, deeper in experience and built around a frontcourt that can score, pass and keep possessions alive.So, for Jon Scheyer's Blue Devils, the first question is simple: can they get the game played on their terms?That concept has been what Jon Scheyer emphasized the most during various media appearances leading into his team's departure for the nation's capital. He said St. John's is "really connected" and "different," adding that "you don't play many teams that press you the whole game." That is the challenge Duke has to solve before anything else offensively can matter.St. John's is 30-6 and enters Friday after winning the Big East regular season and tournament titles. The Red Storm score 81.1 points per game, allow 69.4, own a +3.3 turnover margin and average 38.8 rebounds. The offensive identity is not built around bombing away from 3-point range, but creating extra possessions and pressure points. The KenPom profile shows St. John's is strong on the offensive glass, protects the ball well enough itself and gets to the line at a high rate. That's why so much of this week's narrative has been about why the Red Storm can win ugly.Everything starts with Zuby Ejiofor. He leads St. John's in scoring at 16.3 points, rebounding at 7.3 and also functions as a playmaking hub, with 125 assists and 78 blocks on the season. Bryce Hopkins gives them another experienced scorer at 13.6 points and 6.2 rebounds per game, and Dillon Mitchell is the connective piece who adds 8.2 points, 7.1 rebounds, 108 assists and All Big East defensive value. Oziyah Sellers is the team's most productive volume 3-point shooter, while Ian Jackson and Dylan Darling give the backcourt enough scoring and playmaking to keep the pressure from sitting only on the forwards. Scheyer described Ejiofor and Hopkins as "experienced" and "physical," and said flatly: "their front court is legit."From Duke's side, the challenge is obvious. St. John's will try to turn the game into a ball pressure exercise for 40 minutes instead of letting it become a halfcourt affair. Duke's turnover numbers are solid rather than dominant, and that matters against a defense that can speed possessions up. Scheyer said Duke's offense "has to help your defense" against the way St. John's guards. That is just another way of saying careless possessions will not just cost Duke shots; they will fuel the part of St. John's offense that is hardest to defend.That puts Cayden Boozer in a central role, maybe THE central role of this game. Scheyer said the freshman's "composure" has stood out and noted he has a 5-to-1 assist-to-turnover ratio in the NCAA tournament to date, and the Blue Devils need that version of Boozer Friday. It also may need Cameron Boozer, Nikolas Khamenia, and maybe a few others to help initiate offense and keep St. John's from loading the full burden onto one ballhandler. If Duke can break pressure early and get into offense with space, the rest of the matchup shifts.Because once Duke gets the game into the frontcourt, there are reasons to like the Blue Devils' side of things.The biggest is size and rebounding. Duke averages 40.4 rebounds per game and owns a +11.1 margin. The Blue Devils rank among the nation's best on the offensive glass, while St. John's has been more vulnerable on the defensive backboards than a team with its size might suggest. That could be a real opening for Cameron Boozer, an improving Patrick Ngongba and Maliq Brown. If Duke turns misses into second shots, it can punish the very aggression St. John's uses to create disruption.Building off that, the second reason to like Scheyer's squad is Duke's efficiency inside the arc. The Blue Devils have been one of the country's best 2-point offenses all year, which matters against a St. John's defense that thrives when it can create chaos before a shot goes up. If Duke can get through the first wave and make St. John's defend multiple actions, the Blue Devils have the frontcourt scoring and passing to find good looks near the rim.Which leads us to the other side of the match-up which Scheyer alluded to. Duke's defense has been the best unit in the country by adjusted efficiency per KenPom. St. John's is effective offensively, but the season long numbers say the Red Storm are not a dominant shooting team, in fact they are prone to droughts. They are more dangerous when they are living on second chances, turnovers and free throws. Duke's defense is elite at limiting free throw attempts and strong on the defensive glass. If those traits hold, St. John's will have to beat Duke with half court out of character shot making more often than it wants.If you want the quick summary of it all, St.John's wants a chaotic evening: pressure, deflections, offensive rebounds, bodies at the foul line, and Duke having to restart possessions farther from the basket than it prefers. Duke, meanwhile, needs a quieter game with fewer live ball turnovers, defensive rebounds and more halfcourt possessions in which its size and efficiency can show up.There's also the health variable for the Blue Devils. Scheyer said Caleb Foster has "an outside chance maybe for Friday," while also cautioning that Patrick Ngongba is "not close to 100%." Even so, Scheyer said Ngongba's impact can be felt simply by being on the floor. That is a big variable for his team against Ejiofor and Hopkins. A healthy Foster would give Duke another experienced ballhandler against the press. A useful Ngongba gives Duke another big body who can pass and another interior option in a game that should be decided around the lane and the backboards.So what turns the game? Three things stand out.Duke has to keep its turnover number manageable. They didn't do that at the usual levels against Siena and TCU. Second, it has to win enough of the rebounding battle to keep St. John's from stacking extra possessions. Third, Duke has to defend without letting the game become a parade to the foul line for the Red Storm.Do those three things and the Blue Devils will be favored thanks to their size, half-court defense, interior efficiency and Cameron Boozer's all-around control of a game. If St. John's wins the possession battle with pressure and offensive rebounding, then Duke will spend the night playing catch-up, which is exactly where the Red Storm want this game to live.Ultimately we expect a battle, but think Duke will meet the challenge head on and move on to the Elite Eight. And so the pick...Duke 73, St. John's 67
